impact.location_description: Greenland Sea, roughly 100 km south/southwest of Jan Mayen island, between Greenland and Svalbard
impact.context: Remote Arctic ocean at night; nearest inhabited land (Jan Mayen) uninhabited except a small Norwegian meteorological/military station.

meteorites.notes: Deep Arctic ocean impact; no recovery attempted.

sensor_detections: Infrasound at station I37NO (northern Iceland) and I18DK (Greenland), yielding an independent estimate around 2-4 kt
confirmation.eyewitness: A possible flash reported from northern Iceland; unconfirmed.

scientific_results: 2022 EB5 was the first imminent impactor discovered by a European observer/telescope (Sárneczky, Hungary), and the fifth pre-impact discovery overall, establishing Konkoly Observatory's small 0.6 m Schmidt as a credible contributor to the imminent-impactor discovery rate previously dominated by Catalina and Pan-STARRS.

The roughly order-of-magnitude spread between the ~3.8 kt sensor-measured energy and the ~0.4 kt ESA-modeled energy (from the tracked size/speed alone) is one of the largest measured/modeled discrepancies in the 13-object set, illustrating how uncertain absolute-magnitude-to-size-to-energy conversions remain for meter-class bodies.
Multi-station infrasound triangulation (Iceland + Greenland) provided an independent cross-check on the US sensor energy estimate, of a kind normally reserved for nuclear-test monitoring.
narrative: Krisztián Sárneczky spotted a fast-moving object with the Piszkéstető Schmidt telescope at 19:24 UTC on 11 March 2022, and within roughly two hours automated hazard-assessment systems confirmed a near-certain impact in the far North Atlantic. The object entered at 21:22:45 UTC southwest of the remote Norwegian island of Jan Mayen, producing an atmospheric explosion recorded by US government sensors at about 3.8 kt and cross-checked by infrasound arrays in Iceland and Greenland. No meteorites were recoverable from the deep Arctic ocean, and the only possible visual sighting -- a flash reported from northern Iceland -- was never confirmed. As the fifth of the 13 pre-impact discoveries and the first made by a European team, 2022 EB5 demonstrated that modest-aperture Old World telescopes could compete with the large American surveys for these fleeting detections.
